name: Stein Winch Kit for RCW 3001
title: Stein Winch Kit for RCW 3001 Lowering Device
meta: The Stein winch kit for the RCW 3001 adds winch parts to the rigging control winch, so one device can lower wood and take up slack or tension on the rope.
tagline: Winch parts for the Stein RCW 3001, for crews that lower and pull with one device.
summary: The Stein winch kit for the RCW 3001 is an add-on for the Stein rigging control winch, the trunk-mounted lowering device. It lets the same unit take in slack and put tension on a line as well as let wood down under friction.
highlights: Add-on kit for the Stein RCW 3001
Lets one device lower and winch
Useful for pre-tensioning and directional pulls
Mounts on an existing RCW 3001 setup
specs: Per Stein documentation for the RCW 3001

p: A rigging control winch earns its keep when it can do more than lower. With the winch parts fitted, the RCW 3001 can pull slack out of the rigging line, snug a piece before the cut, and help put a little tension on a leader you want to steer. It saves rigging a separate puller for small jobs.

Check the listing and your unit before ordering, so you know exactly which components are in the box and that they match your RCW 3001. Browse other lowering devices if you are still choosing a system.

Mount the device to a sound trunk with a sling rated for the job, keep hands clear of the drum, and only winch with the device locked in a controlled state. Lowering forces on big wood can be far higher than the piece weighs, so plan the rigging point and line size accordingly.

Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years. Read Stein's instructions before first use and keep them with the device.

faq.q: Does this kit replace the RCW 3001?
faq.a: No. It is an add-on for an existing Stein RCW 3001, giving it winch capability alongside lowering.

faq.q: Can I use the winch for life support?
faq.a: No. It is rigging equipment for controlling and pulling loads, not for raising or lowering people.

name: Fiddle Block Set with 120 ft Rope
title: Fiddle Block Set with 120 ft Rope for Tree Work
h1: Fiddle Block Set with 120 ft Rope
meta: A fiddle block set reeved with 120 ft of rope for pulling trees, tensioning lines and freeing hung tops. A ready mechanical advantage system for crews.
tagline: A rope-and-block pulling system with 120 ft of line, rigged and ready for the truck.
summary: This fiddle block set comes reeved with 120 ft of rope, giving a crew a ready mechanical advantage system for pulling, tensioning and lifting. Hook one block to an anchor and the other to the load, and you multiply what the ground crew can pull.
highlights: Fiddle blocks reeved with 120 ft of rope
Multiplies pulling force for the ground crew
Self-contained system that stores in a bag
Pairs with slings for quick anchors
specs: See markings on blocks and rope

p: A fiddle block set is the go-to when you need a steady, controlled pull: leaning a tree into the lay, tensioning a speedline, pulling a hung top free, or snugging a rigging line before a cut. Because the rope is already reeved through the blocks, setup is fast, and the system goes back in its bag at the end of the day.

The 120 ft of rope sets how far the blocks can open. A longer set gives more travel between anchor and load, which helps on bigger pulls and wider drop zones. See the rest of our mechanical advantage gear for other ratios and sizes.

Anchor to something stronger than the pull, use slings rated for the load, and keep the crew out of the line of the rope in case anything lets go. Pull steadily rather than in jerks, and remember that a mechanical advantage system can overload a weak anchor or rigging point without anyone feeling it.

Inspect the blocks for cracked sheaves, worn axles and bent side plates, and the rope for cuts and glazing. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What is a fiddle block?
faq.a: A block with two sheaves of different sizes, one above the other. A pair of them reeved together gives a compact pulley system for pulling and tensioning.

faq.q: Is 120 ft of rope enough?
faq.a: It depends on how far apart the anchor and load are. The blocks can only open as far as the rope allows, so measure your typical setup before choosing a length.

name: Fiddle Block Set without Rope
title: Fiddle Blocks Set without Rope for Arborist Pulls
meta: A pair of fiddle blocks sold without rope, so you can reeve them with your own line and length. A compact mechanical advantage set for pulls and tensioning.
tagline: A pair of fiddle blocks without rope, for crews who want to choose their own line.
summary: This set of fiddle blocks comes without rope, so you can reeve them with the line diameter and length that suits your work. It is also the right buy when the rope on an existing set has worn out and the blocks are still good.
highlights: Pair of fiddle blocks, no rope
Reeve with your own line and length
Replaces blocks or builds a custom system
specs: Sold separately; match diameter to the sheaves

p: Plenty of crews already have good rope on hand, or want a longer or shorter system than the ready-made sets. Buying the blocks alone lets you reeve them with the right length for how far your anchors usually sit from the load, and replace just the rope when it wears.

Choose a rope that fits the sheaves properly. Line that is too fat will bind and wear; line that is too thin can jump the sheave. Our mechanical advantage section has complete sets if you would rather start rigged.

Reeve the blocks so the rope runs without twisting, and test the system with a light pull before putting real load on it. Keep the crew out of the line of pull, and think about what the pull is doing to the anchor, which sees more than the haul team feels.

Check sheaves for cracks and grooves, axles for wear and side plates for bending before each use. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What rope should I use with these blocks?
faq.a: Use a rope diameter that matches the sheaves, as marked on the blocks or in the maker's instructions, with a strength suited to the pulls you plan.

faq.q: Can I use them to replace blocks on an old set?
faq.a: Yes, if the rope is still in good shape and fits the sheaves. Inspect the rope carefully before reusing it.

name: Maasdam Continuous Rope Puller Replacement Kit
title: Maasdam Rope Puller Replacement Kit
h1: Maasdam Continuous Rope Puller Replacement Kit
meta: Replacement kit for the Maasdam rope puller, continuous style. Service a worn puller and keep it pulling trees, hung tops and loads instead of buying a new one.
tagline: Service parts to bring a worn Maasdam rope puller back into work.
summary: The Maasdam rope puller replacement kit lets you service a Maasdam continuous rope puller rather than replace the whole tool. When the puller starts slipping or the parts show wear, a kit like this is the cheap way back to a working puller.
highlights: Service kit for Maasdam rope pullers
Keep one in the truck with the puller

body.h: Keeping a rope puller in service
p: A Maasdam rope puller is a simple hand-operated tool for pulling a tree over, freeing a hung top or tensioning a line, and like any tool that grips rope under load, its working parts wear. When the puller starts to slip or the action feels rough, swapping in fresh parts is usually all it needs.
Check your puller's model and the kit contents before ordering so the parts match. You will find other pulling and mechanical advantage gear in the same section.

Follow Maasdam's instructions for replacing parts, and test the puller under a light load before you trust it on a real pull. Use rope of the size and type the puller was designed for, because the wrong rope will slip or wear the grip quickly.

Rope pullers can build a lot of force. Anchor to something sound, keep people out of the line of pull and well back from the tree, and stop if anything shifts. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: How do I know my puller needs the kit?
faq.a: If the puller slips under load, the action feels rough, or parts are visibly worn or damaged, it is time to service it or take it out of use.

faq.q: Will this fit every Maasdam puller?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Confirm your model against the kit before ordering.

name: Petzl JAG Double Pulley
title: Petzl JAG Double Pulley for Haul Systems
meta: The Petzl JAG is a compact double pulley with a becket, made for building haul and mechanical advantage systems. A light pulley for arborist pulls and rigging.
tagline: A compact double pulley with becket for building light haul systems.
summary: The Petzl JAG is a double pulley with a becket attachment point, built for setting up compact mechanical advantage systems. Arborists use it for tensioning lines, small pulls and haul setups where a big fiddle block would be overkill.
highlights: Two sheaves side by side plus a becket
Compact and light for the saddle or bag
Pairs with a second pulley for a basic haul kit

p: The JAG is small enough to live in a gear bag and quick to set up. Paired with another pulley and a length of rope, it makes a compact system for tensioning a speedline, snugging a guy line, or putting a controlled pull on a small leader before a cut.

The becket gives you a place to tie off the rope end or attach a second pulley, which is how you build more advantage from a small kit. Compare it with heavier blocks in our mechanical advantage range.

The JAG is a small pulley. It is not a substitute for a rigging block when you are catching and lowering wood, because the dynamic forces in rigging are far higher than a steady pull. Use it for controlled hauling and tensioning within Petzl's ratings.

Check the sheaves turn freely and the side plates are not cracked or bent, and keep it clean of sap and grit. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What is the becket for?
faq.a: It is an attachment point on the pulley where you tie off the rope end or clip a second pulley to build a haul system.

faq.q: Can I use the JAG as a rigging block?
faq.a: No. It is meant for hauling and tensioning, not for catching dynamic loads when rigging wood down.

name: CMI Speed Line Kit
title: CMI Speed Line Kit for Moving Brush and Wood
meta: The CMI speed line kit gives a crew the hardware to rig a speedline and zip brush and wood out of the tree to a drop zone, away from roofs, fences and gardens.
tagline: Hardware to set up a speedline and send brush and wood to a clear drop zone.
summary: The CMI speed line kit gathers the hardware a crew needs to rig a speedline, a tensioned line that carries brush and wood out of the tree to a clear drop zone. It is a time saver on jobs where you cannot drop anything under the tree.
highlights: Moves brush and wood over obstacles
Cuts down on rigging and lowering time

p: On a tight backyard job, the hard part is often not cutting the wood but getting it to the ground somewhere safe. A speedline runs from high in the tree to an anchor near the chipper or drop zone. Each piece is clipped on and rides down the line, over the roof, fence or flower beds below.
A kit saves you from hunting down matched parts. Check the listing for exactly what is included and add slings or a tensioning system as needed. More kits are in our rigging kits section.

Speedlines put big loads on both anchors, and the more you tension the line, the higher those forces get. Choose sound anchors, keep the angle sensible, control the speed of each piece, and keep everyone clear of the line and the landing zone.

Inspect pulleys, connectors and rope before each use. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What can I send down a speedline?
faq.a: Brush and manageable wood that the line, hardware and anchors are rated for. Large wood belongs on a lowering system.

faq.q: How tight should the line be?
faq.a: Only as tight as needed for clearance. Over-tensioning multiplies the load on the anchors and hardware.

name: ISC 1/2 in. Rigging Block with Sling
title: ISC Rigging Block, 1/2 in., with Sling Kit
h1: ISC 1/2 in. Rigging Block with Sling
meta: An ISC rigging block sized for 1/2 inch rigging rope, paired with a sling to hang it. A ready rigging block kit for arborists lowering limbs and smaller wood.
tagline: An ISC rigging block for 1/2 inch line, with a sling to hang it.
summary: This ISC rigging block kit pairs a block sized for 1/2 inch rigging line with a sling to hang it in the tree. It is a practical setup for lowering limbs and moderate wood where a natural crotch would chew up the rope.
highlights: Sling included for hanging the block
Reduces rope wear versus natural crotch rigging
Sized for limbs and moderate wood
specs: See markings on block and sling

p: Running a rigging line over a natural crotch is fine for small wood, but it builds friction, wears the rope and can damage the tree. A block hung on a sling gives the line a clean path, lets the ground crew control descent at the lowering device, and makes the rigging point easier to predict.
This kit is sized for 1/2 inch line, a common size for everyday pruning and smaller removals. See our rigging kits for larger setups.

Hang the block above the work on a sound stem, close to the trunk, with the sling choked or wrapped as the maker intends. Make sure the rope fits the sheave, and keep the block and sling within their rated loads, remembering that dynamic loads from dropping wood are many times the piece weight.

Check the sheave turns freely, the side plates are not bent, and the sling is free of cuts and glazing. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What rope does this block take?
faq.a: It is sized for 1/2 inch rigging rope. Do not run larger line through it.

faq.q: Is a 1/2 inch setup big enough for removals?
faq.a: It suits limbs and moderate wood. Heavy wood and big tops call for larger blocks, slings and rope.

name: ISC 5/8 in. Aluminum Rigging Block with 5/8 in. Dead-Eye Sling
title: ISC Aluminum Rigging Block 5/8 in. with Dead-Eye Sling
h1: ISC 5/8 in. Aluminum Rigging Block with 5/8 in. Dead-Eye Sling
meta: ISC aluminum rigging block for 5/8 inch rope, paired with a 5/8 inch dead-eye sling. A light, ready rigging setup for arborists lowering limbs and wood.
tagline: A light aluminum rigging block for 5/8 inch line with a matching dead-eye sling.
summary: This kit pairs an ISC aluminum rigging block for 5/8 inch rope with a 5/8 inch dead-eye sling to hang it. The aluminum body keeps the weight down for the climber who has to carry it up, while the sling makes it quick to set.
highlights: Aluminum block keeps weight down aloft
specs: See markings on block and sling

p: Every pound on the saddle counts on a long climb. An aluminum block is lighter than steel of similar size, so it is easier to take aloft and hang. Paired with a dead-eye sling, it sets quickly: wrap the sling around the stem, pass the tail through the eye and clip the block.
5/8 inch line is a good all-round size for removals and heavier pruning, and matching the block and sling to it keeps the system consistent. Browse more rigging kits for other sizes.

Hang the block close to the trunk on a sound stem above the work, and size the whole system, block, sling, rope and lowering device, to the wood you plan to catch. Aluminum is lighter but can wear and gouge, so watch the sheave and side plates closely.

Inspect the sling for cuts, glazing and a damaged eye before each job. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: Why aluminum rather than steel?
faq.a: Aluminum saves weight for the climber. Steel blocks are heavier but can better tolerate wear and abuse.

faq.q: How does a dead-eye sling attach?
faq.a: Wrap it around the stem, pass the tail through the eye to form a choke, and clip the block to the tail end.

name: Port-a-Wrap with 5/8 in. Whoopie Sling
title: Port-a-Wrap with 5/8 in. Whoopie Sling Kit
meta: A port-a-wrap friction lowering device paired with a 5/8 inch whoopie sling that adjusts to the trunk. A quick-mounting lowering kit for tree removal crews.
tagline: A friction lowering device and an adjustable 5/8 inch whoopie sling to mount it.
summary: This kit pairs a port-a-wrap with a 5/8 inch whoopie sling, so the lowering device and its adjustable mount come together. The whoopie sling tightens to fit the trunk, which makes setup at the base of the tree quick.
highlights: Friction lowering device plus mounting sling
Whoopie sling adjusts to trunk diameter
Fast setup at the base of the tree

p: A whoopie sling is an adjustable sling: pull the tail and the loop shrinks to snug against the trunk. That makes it easy to mount the port-a-wrap at a comfortable working height on trunks of different sizes without carrying several fixed slings.
The port-a-wrap itself is a simple friction device: the ground worker takes wraps around it to control how fast wood comes down. See more rigging kits for other device and sling pairings.

Mount the sling snug on the trunk, clip the device so the line feeds straight on, and take enough wraps for the load. Keep the tail controlled and stand clear of the rope path. Heavy wood generates loads far beyond its weight, so add wraps rather than fighting the rope.

Check the sling for cuts, glazing and a worn bury, and the device for grooves and cracks, before each job. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What does the whoopie sling do?
faq.a: It adjusts in length, so you can snug it around trunks of different sizes and set the port-a-wrap at the height you want.

faq.q: How many wraps should I take?
faq.a: Enough to control the load comfortably. Heavier wood needs more wraps; train ground workers on the device before they lower real wood.

name: 1/2 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling for Port-a-Wrap, 8 ft
title: 1/2 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling for Port-a-Wrap, 8 ft
h1: 1/2 in. Soft Anchor Rigging Sling for Port-a-Wrap, 8 ft
meta: A 1/2 inch by 8 ft soft anchor rigging sling for mounting a port-a-wrap to the trunk. Light, bark-friendly and quick to set for everyday lowering setups.
tagline: A 1/2 in. soft sling for anchoring lowering devices and blocks without hardware.
summary: This 1/2 in. soft anchor rigging sling gives you a quick, bark-friendly way to anchor rigging to a trunk or stem. It is sized and intended for mounting a port-a-wrap at the base of the tree.
highlights: No steel to carry or snag

p: A soft anchor sling wraps around the stem and holds its connection by the way it is formed, not by a steel shackle or ring. That keeps the weight down, spreads load over the bark, and makes it quick to set and remove.
At the base of the tree, it is a clean way to mount a port-a-wrap without chains or straps. More options are in our adjustable slings section.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands. Look for cut or pulled strands, glazed or melted fibers, flat or stiff spots, and heavy UV fading, and check that the splices and buries are intact. Retire it if you find damage you can't explain or after a shock load bigger than you planned for.

Match the sling diameter to the rest of the system and keep it within its rating. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: Why use a soft sling instead of a chain or strap?
faq.a: It is lighter, gentler on bark, easy to adjust to the trunk and quick to inspect.

faq.q: How do I know the sling's strength?
faq.a: Check the tag on the sling and the product listing, and keep it within that rating with a working margin.

name: 3/4 in. Whoopie Ring Sling with XL Ring
title: 3/4 in. Whoopie Ring Sling with XL Ring
h1: 3/4 in. Whoopie Ring Sling with XL Ring
meta: A 3/4 inch whoopie ring sling with an XL ring, giving an adjustable, low-friction rigging point that sets on stems of many sizes for limbs and redirects.
tagline: An adjustable whoopie sling with an XL ring for a smooth rigging point.
summary: This 3/4 in. whoopie ring sling combines an adjustable whoopie body with an XL ring, giving a smooth, low-friction rigging point that fits stems of different sizes.
highlights: Adjustable whoopie body fits many stem sizes
XL ring for a smooth rope path
Light compared with a steel block
Retrievable setups possible with the right rigging
specs: Adjustable whoopie sling with XL ring
See tag on sling and ring markings

p: A whoopie sling adjusts by sliding the tail through a hollow-braid section; under load the braid grips and holds the length. Put a large ring on it and you have a light rigging point the rope can run through, or a place to clip a block.
The XL ring gives the rope a broad radius to run over, which is easier on line than a small ring. See more adjustable slings for other sizes.

Set the sling snug around a sound stem and keep the ring loaded in line, not side-loaded across a crotch. A ring builds more friction than a block, which helps on small wood but adds wear, so watch the rope and ring surface.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands. Look for cut or pulled strands, glazed or melted fibers, flat or stiff spots, and heavy UV fading, and check that the splices and buries are intact. summary: The 1/2 in. spider leg balancing sling has several legs joined at one point, so you can attach a piece at more than one spot and control how it hangs. It is the tool for lowering or picking a limb level instead of letting it swing butt-first.

p: A limb tied at one point will hang from that point, usually butt-down, and swing. With a spider leg sling you can tie into the limb at two or more places and lower it close to level. That matters over a roof, between obstacles, or when you need the piece to land in a tight spot.
The 1/2 in. size handles heavier limbs and moderate picks. See more heavy-duty slings for other rigging slings.

faq.a: When a piece needs to come down level or in a controlled attitude, such as over a roof or into a tight landing zone.

faq.a: Rarely. Leg angles and attachment points change the share, so size the sling with a good margin.

summary: This dead-eye ring sling comes with a Beast ring, a large rigging ring, for a smooth, heavy-duty rigging point. Choke the sling on the stem through its eye and run the rigging line through the ring or clip a block.
highlights: Dead-eye sling with a large ring
Lighter than a big steel block
specs: See tag on sling and ring markings

body.h: A big ring for heavy work
p: A large ring gives the rigging line a broad radius to run over, which is kinder to the rope than a small ring and builds useful friction at the top. Hung on a dead-eye sling, it makes a rigging point that is light, strong and quick to set.
Check the listing for the sling diameter and length so it matches your rigging line. See our heavy-duty slings for other options.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands. Look for cut or pulled strands, glazed or melted fibers, flat or stiff spots, and heavy UV fading, and check that the splices and buries are intact. Retire it if you find damage you can't explain or after a shock load bigger than you planned for. Check the ring for gouges, sharp edges and deep wear grooves, and retire it if the rope surface is no longer smooth.

Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: What is a Beast ring?
faq.a: A large rigging ring designed for running rope over it in friction rigging setups, or for attaching a block.

faq.q: Does a ring replace a block?
faq.a: For some work. Rings add friction and save weight; blocks run freer for heavy, repeated lowering.

name: Retrievable Ring Sling, 3/4 in.
title: Retrievable Ring Sling, 3/4 in., for Rigging
meta: A 3/4 in. retrievable ring sling you can set as a rigging point and pull down from the ground after the work. Saves a climb back up just to recover the sling.
tagline: A 3/4 in. ring sling you can set and retrieve from the ground.
summary: This 3/4 in. retrievable ring sling uses rings so the sling can be set as a rigging point and then pulled down from the ground when the work is done. It saves a climb back up just to collect the sling.
highlights: Saves a climb to recover gear
specs: See tag on sling and ring markings

p: On a job where the rigging point is high and the climber is coming down, a retrievable sling can be collected from the ground. The rings let the sling choke the stem under load and then release and pull through when it is unloaded and you pull the right leg.
The 3/4 in. size handles heavier rigging work. See all heavy-duty slings for other options.
Rig it the way the maker intends, and practice retrieval low to the ground before you rely on it. Make sure the retrieval path is clear of branches that could snag it.

Before each job, run the sling through your hands. Look for cut or pulled strands, glazed or melted fibers, flat or stiff spots, and heavy UV fading, and check that the splices and buries are intact. Retire it if you find damage you can't explain or after a shock load bigger than you planned for. Rigging gear is for moving wood, not for life support. Match every component to the load with a working margin, follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, and make sure the crew is trained in rigging before relying on it. Note when each piece went into service, so worn gear gets retired on time instead of living on the truck for years.

faq.q: How does a retrievable ring sling come down?
faq.a: Once unloaded, you pull the retrieval end and the sling releases from the stem and falls clear, so it must be rigged as the maker instructs.

faq.q: Can I use it for life support?
faq.a: No. It is rigging equipment for loads only.
